newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dlr mostly steady in Tokyo after trade data.
newsitem.headline: Dlr mostly steady in Tokyo after trade data.

text.p: 0300 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0300 GMT
The dollar was mostly steady by midday Tokyo, despite the release of closely watched trade data, which showed a dramatic rise in Japan's surplus for the second month in a row in May.
Solid bids from Japanese investors, including Japan's public investment bodies, at below 113.00 yen and concerns about North Korea inhibited the dollar's decline, dealers said.
Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus, often the source of bitter rows with the United States, jumped more than 200 percent in May from a year earlier to 738.27 billion yen.
The dollar briefly dipped on the data as traders felt the increase was larger than what the market had expected, but the decline was short-lived due to a lack of followthrough selling.

"The surplus was huge but roughly within the higher range of expectations," said a Japanese bank trader. The surplus with the U.S., which has already been grumbling about the growing trade imbalance between the two countries, surged 93 percent in May from a year earlier to 322.87 billion yen.

North Korea on Wednesday warned it was ready for a "final battle" with the U.S and South Korea, which it claimed were on the verge of attacking the impoverished and famine-stricken communist state. The news helped the dollar slightly, with a rise in tension in the Korean peninsula seen as a dollar-buying factor, dealers said.
But lingering selling pressure from overseas operators and Japanese exporters checked the dollar's rebound.
Traders were completely split over the dollar/yen's direction, with some saying Japan's trade surplus could continue to be a major dollar selling factor before the summit.

"We still can't make any final judgment based on two or three months or even a quarter, but the numbers do reinforce our concern that the surplus appears to be climbing again and that this year there may be a significant increase in Japan's trade surplus," a U.S. official in Tokyo told Reuters.
Some traders were betting that Japan would be forced to accept a higher yen to curb its trade surplus, even though a stronger yen would be negative for Japan's economy.
Others were thinking that the market has already factored in the trade issue and that it would not become a major factor to drag the dollar substantially lower.
"Opinions were completely split over the dollar/yen's direction. In my view, the dollar is likely to stay in a 110-117 yen range for the next month," said a trader at another European bank.
The dollar closed at 113.28/33 yen and 1.7305/10 marks in New York on Monday.
